name: DEWINE, J.
description: Concurred, arguing that Ohio's non-spousal artificial insemination statute does not apply to unmarried couples and that U.S. Supreme Court precedent does not empower courts to retroactively rewrite the statute to include them or to conduct a "would have been married" inquiry.

name: BRUNNER, J.
description: Concurred in judgment only, arguing that the First District erred by considering an unpreserved issue and the Supreme Court should have reversed on that procedural ground without reaching the merits of the appeal.

name: DEWINE, J.
description: Concurred, arguing that the Ohio Constitution's command to pay compensation for taken property applies regardless of whether the property is within the taking municipality's boundaries, thus granting standing for an inverse-condemnation claim.

name: DEWINE, J.
description: Concurred, authored the opinion of the court, arguing that police officers can be victims under Marsy's Law, and therefore their identifying information can be redacted from public records.

name: FISCHER, J.
description: Concurred in part and dissented in part, arguing that officers can be victims under Marsy's Law and their information can be redacted, but the Dispatch is entitled to other unredacted footage from officers not deemed victims and that the court should have applied statutes in effect at the time of the public-records request.

name: BRUNNER, J.
description: Concurred in part and dissented in part, arguing that police officers can be victims but that the Ohio Constitution guarantees a right to access government information, and R.C. 2930.07 is unconstitutional as applied, requiring unredacted footage of police officers in public duty.

name: MENTEL, J.
description: Concurred, argued that the noneconomic damages cap in R.C. 2323.43 is unconstitutional as applied to the plaintiff's case, violating her rights to due process and equal protection.

name: DEWINE, J.
description: Concurred, authored the opinion of the court, arguing that Martens lacked standing because the Sheward public-right doctrine was an aberration that should be overruled, and he failed to establish taxpayer standing.

name: BRUNNER, J.
description: Concurred in judgment only, arguing that Martens lacked standing but that overruling the Sheward public-right doctrine was unnecessary and procedurally inappropriate in this case.

name: FISCHER, J.
description: Concurred, argued that the court should have ordered supplemental briefing on the adversity issue, but on the merits, R.C. 3705.15 only permits corrections for errors at the time of birth, not for changes arising after birth, thus affirming the lower court's denial.

name: DONNELLY, J.
description: Concurred, argued that the court should have reached the merits of the case and affirmed the lower court's decision because R.C. 3705.15 does not permit correcting a sex marker on a birth certificate for a transgender person based on changes after birth.

name: BRUNNER, J.
description: Dissented, argued that R.C. 3705.15's plain language confers authority on probate courts to correct a sex marker on any person's birth record, including for transgender individuals, and that denying such applications is unconstitutional discrimination.

name: DETERS, J.
description: Dissented, argued that the appeal lacked adversity because no other party had a legal interest that would be diminished by granting the application, and therefore the court of appeals lacked judicial power to decide the appeal.

name: DEWINE, J.
description: Concurred, argued that the Ohio Constitution's open courts provision mandates individualized balancing for sealing juvenile records, rendering the blanket sealing statute unconstitutional.

name: DONNELLY, J.
description: Concurred in judgment only, argued that the majority's analysis was unnecessarily broad and contained erroneous legal conclusions, but agreed with the final outcome.

name: STEWART, J.
description: Dissented, argued that the Enquirer had no clear right to the records as the statute mandated sealing, and the majority's novel interpretation was flawed and judicially activist.

name: KENNEDY, C.J.
description: Concurred, argued that the same-juror rule applies in all negligence cases where sequential interrogatories separate the elements of negligence, requiring the same three-fourths of jurors to concur on all elements for a valid verdict.

name: BRUNNER, J.
description: Dissented, argued that the majority's application of the same-juror rule upends over 30 years of precedent and erodes the fundamental right to a trial by a full jury, and that the any-majority rule should apply to non-apportionment questions like negligence and proximate cause.

name: FISCHER, J.

name: DONNELLY, J.

name: STEWART, J.

name: BRUNNER, J.

name: DEWINE, J.
description: Concurred, argued that the trial court erred by allowing remote testimony without sufficient case-specific findings of necessity, but this error was harmless given the overwhelming evidence of guilt.

name: FISCHER, J.

name: Kennedy, C.J.

name: Kennedy, C.J.

name: Fischer, J.

name: Fischer, J.

name: Donnelly, J.

name: Stewart, J.
description: Dissented, concurred with Justice Donnelly's dissenting opinion.

name: Brunner, J.

name: DEWINE, J.

name: BRUNNER, J.

name: STEWART, J.

name: BRUNNER, J.

name: DONNELLY, J.

name: FISCHER, J.
description: Dissented, argued that R.C. 2909.15(D)(2)(b) violates the separation-of-powers doctrine by delegating judicial authority to the executive branch, allowing prosecutors and law enforcement to control a trial court's discretion in sentencing regarding arson registration periods.

name: Stewart

name: Brunner, J.

name: DONNELLY, J.

name: STEWART, J.

name: BRUNNER, J.
description: Concurred in part and dissented in part, arguing that the ballot language must more clearly explain the different amendment standards for citizen initiatives versus legislative proposals to prevent misleading voters.

name: Kennedy, C.J.

name: Kennedy, J.
description: Dissented, argued that the majority opinion overreaches judicial authority by substituting its policy preferences for the General Assembly's legislative decisions and that Brandt failed to prove the statute was unconstitutional as applied.

description: Concurred, argued that the claim for a jury trial fails due to the lack of a historical analogue and because it is inconsistent with the state's limited waiver of sovereign immunity.

name: DONNELLY, J.
description: Dissented, argued that a constitutional right to a jury trial exists in an action under R.C. 2743.48 to be declared a wrongfully imprisoned person.

description: Concurred, argued that victims forfeited their right to restitution by not appealing the initial denial, and the trial court lost jurisdiction to impose restitution after the sentence was final.

description: Concurred, argued that the trial court lacked jurisdiction to modify the sentence, which violated the Double Jeopardy Clause.

name: DeWine, J.
description: Concurred, argued that the trial court lacked jurisdiction and violated Brasher's Double Jeopardy rights by modifying the sentence after it was final.

name: Stewart, J.
description: Concurred, argued that the trial court's failure to consider Morris's youth as a mitigating factor rendered his life sentence cruel and unusual punishment, upholding State v. Patrick as not overruled by Jones v. Mississippi.

name: FISCHER, J.
description: Dissented, argued that the majority incorrectly upheld State v. Patrick, which was effectively overruled by Jones v. Mississippi, and that federal law does not require explicit consideration of a juvenile's age on the record.

name: Brunner, J.
description: Concurred, argued that R.C. 2152.84(A)(2)(b) is fundamentally unfair as applied to D.R. because it removes judicial discretion at a critical stage, violating due process and undermining the rehabilitative purpose of the juvenile justice system.

name: Fischer, J.
description: Dissented, argued that R.C. 2152.84 complies with due process because no existing protected substantive right is at stake at the completion-of-disposition stage, and the majority's decision legislates from the bench.

name: DeWine, J.
description: Dissented, argued that the law requiring 16- and 17-year-olds to register as sex offenders for three years is constitutional and that the majority misapplies procedural due process to what is a substantive due process claim, effectively legislating from the bench.

name: Kennedy, J.

name: FISCHER, J.
description: Concurred, but only with the judgment, implying a different reasoning than the majority.

name: DeWine, J.
description: Dissented, argued that Haynes forfeited his argument by changing it on appeal and that he suffered no prejudice because all necessary information was available through open-file discovery.

name: Kennedy, J.
description: Dissented, argued that Haynes forfeited his argument and suffered no prejudice from the lack of a bill of particulars due to open-file discovery.

name: Brunner, J.
description: Concurred, argued that Marsy's Law provides a right to "full and timely restitution" but did not alter the meaning of "restitution" in Ohio law, which limits restitution to economic losses directly and proximately caused by the offense, and lost wages for court attendance are not such a direct result.

name: DeWine, J.
description: Dissented, argued that the majority improperly constricts victims' rights by allowing a pre-amendment statute to trump the constitutional right to "full and timely restitution," which should include lost wages for court attendance as a foreseeable consequence of the crime.

name: Fischer, J.
description: Concurred in denying the intervening relators' request but dissented from granting the original relators' request, arguing that neither group of relators demonstrated a clear legal right or duty, and criticized the majority for undermining Ohio law and creating chaos due to prior redistricting decisions, emphasizing that the federal court did not implicitly move filing deadlines.
